name: bluewater-16-the-repair-shop-that-didnt-exist
lines: The top rated repair shop on her map just won her call. The shop does not exist.
Wet towels. Team uniforms. Game tomorrow. And her dryer just died.
She searches. Top of the map, a shop two streets over. Local number. Four point nine stars.
She calls. A friendly voice takes a card number for the visit. Then nobody comes.
Two streets over, there is no shop. Just a pin on a map. And this year, the US government said one company did that more than fifteen thousand times.
Here's what the complaint says. And remember, these are allegations. A court hasn't ruled.
In May, the Justice Department and the state of Illinois sued a home repair company.
They say it built more than fifteen thousand fake business profiles on Google Search and Maps.
Made up company names. Addresses that belonged to other people.
More than seven thousand six hundred phone numbers, each with a local area code.
And fake five star reviews on top.
According to the complaint, the company employed no technicians at all. Calls were answered far away. Some of them overseas.
And the money? The complaint says tens of millions of dollars, from people who thought they were hiring someone local.
Whose calls were those?
Now look at it from the other side of the map.
Meet Omar. He's a made up example. Fourteen years fixing washers and dryers. One van. His name on the side.
He's a real shop, two streets from that fake pin.
Every person who called the fake was looking for somebody like him.
And it isn't one case. Google sued over a separate network last year. About ten thousand fake listings.
So Omar isn't just competing with the shop across town. He's competing with shops that were typed into existence.
The temptation.
That week, an email lands in Omar's inbox.
Fifty five star reviews. Say two hundred dollars. Delivered in a week.
And he thinks, the fakes are doing it. Why am I the only one playing fair?
Here's why. Because the fakers are finally the ones getting caught.
In the US, a federal rule now bans fake reviews outright. Buying them. Writing them. Having staff or family post them without saying who they are.
The fine can run up to fifty three thousand and eighty eight dollars. Per violation.
The first warning letters went out in December twenty twenty five.
Fifty fake reviews isn't a shortcut. It's fifty chances to be fined, with your name on every one.
And Google tightened up too.
Its review rules now spell it out. A business can't offer a discount, a gift, or cash for a review. Any review.
Can't pressure a customer to write one before they leave.
Can't tell them what to say.
Can't give staff a quota. And can't ask only the happy ones.
Break those, and Google says the reviews come down.
What a fake can't copy.
Omar deleted the email. Then he asked a better question. What do I have that a fake listing never will?
One. A face. A fake has a logo and a stock photo. Omar has Omar, standing next to his van.
So put real photos on your listing. You, your truck, your shop. Taken this year.
Two. Real jobs. A before and an after, in a real laundry room.
A fake can invent a review. It can't invent fourteen years of Tuesdays.
Three. One name, one number, one address. The same everywhere. Website, Google, the side of the van.
When a customer checks, a real business matches itself.
Four. Answer every review, in your own voice. A listing with nobody behind it rarely talks back.
Five. Ask every customer, the honest way. After the job. No reward. No script. Everyone, not just the smiling ones.
It's slower. It's also the kind you never have to worry about.
And six. If you spot a fake using your town or your name, report it. Google has a complaint form for misleading listings.
Now the honest part. Being real won't put you at the top of the map by Friday.
And nobody can promise the fakes around you disappear.
But when a customer hesitates between two pins, they look for proof. Be the one that has it.
Back to the dryer. Same wet towels. Same search.
This time she taps the second pin. There's a man in the photo, next to a van with his name on it.
Fourteen years of reviews. And he's answered every one.
She calls. Omar picks up.
You can't out fake a fake. They'll always type faster than you.
So be the one thing on that map they can't copy. Real.
